title: 2026 Construction Outlook Update - Workforce Snapshot
plain_title: Who builds New York, and what the industry wants next
what_they_audited: An annual snapshot from the New York Building Congress, a membership association for the city's building and construction industry, profiling who works in construction in New York City and New York State using 2024 American Community Survey data. It ends with seven proposals aimed at federal, state and city action to widen the pipeline into the trades.
background: The report counts workers in building and infrastructure projects, design, site preparation and excavation, governmental activities and construction consulting, as self-reported in the 2024 American Community Survey. It says the statewide construction workforce has recovered to about 98 percent of its pre-pandemic level and projects a return to pre-pandemic numbers by the end of 2027.

findings.plain: The statewide construction workforce reached 568,000 in 2024, close to the pre-pandemic level of 585,000. New York City accounted for about 45 percent of the state total.
findings.quote: Statewide, the construction workforce rose to 568,000 workers in 2024

findings.plain: The city workforce edged up to 253,000 in 2024, and about three quarters of those workers lived in New York City.

recommendations: Create federal immigration tools for infrastructure work, starting with an H-1B visa cap exemption and fast-track approval program for government-funded infrastructure, targeted at workers educated and trained in the United States in fields such as engineering, architecture, construction management, planning and key technical trades.
Lower the fees for federal certification and required training courses, particularly Occupational Safety and Health Administration training.

Expand Workforce Innovation and Opportunity programs, including the Youth Activities program, the Adult Employment and Training Activities program and the Dislocated Worker Employment and Training Activities program.

Expand career and technical education in New York public schools to prepare students for architecture, engineering and technology careers, and put more money into science, technology, engineering and math education for children and professionals.
Keep building on the New York Building Congress Young Professionals Committee's work recruiting and retaining younger workers in construction.
Increase minority- and women-owned business enterprise participation statewide by building a single place where those firms can bid on state, city and public authority projects.
Create incentives to expand childcare hours so construction families have childcare when they have to be on job sites outside standard working hours.
